howItWorks.intro: This version of the rate math treats your weekly billable-hours estimate — not an annual day count — as the anchor. It grosses up your income target for the share eaten by business expenses, then spreads that grossed-up figure across the hours you'll actually bill in a working year.

rules.name: Hourly Rate
rules.explanation: Target income grossed up for expenses divided by billable hours.

howItWorks.outro: The weekly billable-hours figure you enter is the input worth revisiting most often — track actual invoiced hours for a month or two, compare them to what you typed in here, and recalculate with the real number.

faq.question: Why does this calculator ask for weekly billable hours instead of an annual number?
faq.answer: Because weekly capacity is what you actually experience and can check against reality — pull up your time tracker or last month's invoices and count real billable hours. An annual figure hides the guesswork; a weekly one forces you to be specific about a number you can verify.

faq.question: What's the difference between the hourly rate, day rate, and weekly rate this gives me?
faq.answer: They're the same underlying rate expressed three ways. The hourly rate is your floor per hour. The day rate multiplies it by 8, useful when a client wants to book you for full days. The weekly rate multiplies it by your billable-hours input, useful for retainer or block-time agreements — it assumes you actually bill that many hours that week, not that you're available for 40.

faq.question: How much does underestimating my billable hours actually cost me?
faq.answer: More than most freelancers expect, and it compounds silently. At a $90,000 target with 20% expenses and 4 weeks off, billing 25 hours a week yields roughly $93.75/hr. The same target at 32 billable hours a week drops to about $73.24/hr — a swing of over $20 an hour from a 7-hour difference in a single input.

faq.question: What should I count in "Weeks Off per Year"?
faq.answer: Everything that keeps you from billing: vacation, sick time, the slow month your industry always has, and — the one people forget — the average gap between one contract ending and the next one landing. If that gap runs 2-3 weeks a few times a year, it belongs in this field even though it isn't a planned vacation.

faq.question: Is the "Business Expenses (%)" field the same as self-employment tax?
faq.answer: No — it's whatever share of revenue your specific costs (software, insurance, tax set-asides, equipment, professional fees) actually represent, which you set yourself rather than a fixed rate. If self-employment tax runs roughly 15% of revenue for you and other costs add another 10%, enter 25%, not just the tax portion.

howWeCalculate.intro: The calculator runs three steps in sequence: gross up your income target for expenses, convert your weekly billable-hours estimate into an annual figure using the weeks you're actually working, then divide the first by the second.
steps: Enter your target take-home income and the percentage of revenue you expect business expenses to consume.
Enter the hours you can realistically bill in an average week and how many weeks a year go unbilled between vacation, slow periods, and gaps between contracts.
The calculator grosses up your income target by dividing it by (1 − expense percentage), then multiplies your weekly billable hours by (52 − weeks off) to get annual billable hours.
It divides the grossed-up target by annual billable hours for your minimum hourly rate, then derives the day rate (× 8) and weekly rate (× your billable hours) from it.
howWeCalculate.disclaimer: These figures are a floor, not a target — they show what covers your costs and income goal, not what the market will pay for your particular skill set. Confirm your expense percentage with a bookkeeper or accountant before pricing off it.

whenToUse.intro: Reach for this version of the math when the number you're unsure about is your own capacity, not your income goal.
scenarios: You've never tracked how many hours a week you actually invoice and want to see how sensitive your rate is to that number.
You're quoting a client who wants a day rate or a weekly retainer instead of an hourly figure.
You take real time off between contracts, not just vacation, and want that bench time reflected in your rate.
Your business expenses move as a share of revenue rather than as a flat dollar figure, and a percentage-based expense input fits your situation better than a line-item budget.
You want to stress-test how a few fewer billable hours per week changes what you need to charge before committing to a lighter schedule.

sections.title: What This Calculator Solves For
sections.body: Most freelance rate math starts from an annual salary target and works backward through 260 working days and a fixed vacation allowance. This version skips that detour and asks for the number you actually control week to week: how many hours you can realistically bill in a normal week, and how many weeks a year you expect to go unbilled. Enter your income target, that weekly billable-hours figure, weeks off, and the percentage of revenue eaten by business costs, and the calculator grosses up your target for expenses first, then divides by your annual billable hours — weekly hours multiplied by the weeks you're actually working — to hand back a minimum hourly rate, an 8-hour day rate, and a weekly rate sized to your real billable capacity, not a theoretical 40-hour week.

sections.title: The 25-vs-32 Problem
sections.body: Say you want to take home $90,000, you've budgeted 20% of revenue for expenses (software, insurance, tax set-asides), and you take 4 weeks off a year. If you're honest that you can only bill 25 hours in a typical week — the other 15 go to proposals, revisions, email, and admin — the math runs: $90,000 ÷ 0.80 = $112,500 grossed-up need, divided by 25 hrs × 48 working weeks = 1,200 annual billable hours, giving a minimum hourly rate of $93.75, a day rate of $750, and a weekly rate of $2,343.75. Now rerun it assuming a more optimistic 32 billable hours a week — a number many freelancers write down without ever tracking it. Annual billable hours jump to 1,536, and the same $112,500 need spreads out to just $73.24 an hour. Overestimating your weekly capacity by seven hours quietly discounted your rate by more than 20% — the calculator doesn't know you were optimistic, it just does the division.

sections.title: Weeks Off Isn't Just Vacation
sections.body: Freelancers tend to fill in "weeks off" with whatever paid vacation they'd want as an employee — two or three weeks — and stop there. That undercounts the real unbillable stretches: the week between one contract ending and the next starting, the slow month every industry has, the days lost chasing a late invoice instead of doing billable work. If your actual pattern includes 2 weeks of vacation plus 6 scattered weeks of bench time between projects, put in 8, not 2. Understating weeks off has the same effect as overstating your billable hours — both quietly lower the rate the calculator hands you below what you need to clear your income target once the calendar plays out as it really does, not as a tidy 50-week grind.

howToSteps.title: Set your income target and expense share
howToSteps.description: Enter the annual income you want to clear, then estimate what percentage of your revenue business expenses and taxes will consume.

howToSteps.title: Estimate your real weekly billable hours
howToSteps.description: Enter the hours you can realistically bill in a normal week — not your total desk time, just the hours a client would see on an invoice.

howToSteps.title: Account for weeks you won't bill
howToSteps.description: Enter weeks off covering vacation, slow seasons, and the gaps that typically appear between one contract ending and the next beginning.

howToSteps.title: Compare the hourly, day, and weekly figures
howToSteps.description: Use the minimum hourly rate as your floor, the day rate for day-based engagements, and the weekly rate for retainer conversations.

tips: Track your actual invoiced hours for 4-6 weeks before typing a number into "Billable Hours per Week" — most freelancers guess high.
Set "Weeks Off" to cover every unbilled week you can predict: vacation, the slow season your industry has, and the average gap you see between contracts ending and new ones starting.
If your expenses swing with revenue (payment processing fees, contractor help, ad spend), the percentage-based expense field here fits better than a fixed dollar budget.
Compare the day rate and weekly rate outputs before you quote — a client asking for "3 days a week" should be priced off the day rate, not the hourly rate multiplied loosely.
Recalculate whenever your billable-hours estimate changes by more than a couple of hours a week; it moves your rate more than almost any other input.
